strengths: The main systems contribution is useful and reasonably original: patch-major block-sparse correlation computation, sparse sampling, and cross-iteration caching preserve the RAFT-style operator while targeting the poor memory/runtime trade-off of existing dense and on-demand implementations.

The efficiency evidence is extensive. Isolated experiments cover four GPUs, resolutions up to 8K, iteration counts, and feature dimensions. At 4096-pixel width on A100, the reported sampler uses about 2.9 GB versus 71.3 GB for the dense implementation and runs in 201 ms versus 1932 ms for on-demand sampling.

End-to-end results demonstrate practical impact across several RAFT-family models. For example, native-resolution SEA-RAFT runtime decreases from 2.61 s to 1.90 s, while native-resolution RAFT becomes feasible and decreases from 11.00 s to 4.59 s relative to on-demand sampling.

The proposed cascaded SEA-RAFT inference is simple, training-free, and well motivated by the observed loss of large-motion accuracy at high resolution. On the introduced 8K data, native-resolution cascaded inference substantially improves SEA-RAFT's EPE from 17.63 to 2.70 and large-motion EPE from 107.39 to 21.56.

The paper is generally clear and includes useful component timing, caching ablation, pseudocode, extended per-scale results, and qualitative comparisons. The distinction between benefits at high resolution and overhead at conventional resolutions is reported rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The advertised O(P^1.5) memory complexity is not established for the evaluated implementation. It follows only by choosing block height B=P^(1/8), whereas experiments use fixed B=8 or 16; with fixed B, the full block mask term (P/B^2)^2 remains asymptotically quadratic. No experiment validates adaptive block sizing or its effect on sparsity and kernel efficiency, so the manuscript should distinguish an attainable theoretical configuration from the implemented complexity.

Evidence for exact operator equivalence is limited. The paper reports only a 0.03% downstream endpoint-error difference and mentions unspecified unit tests, without direct maximum/mean numerical-error measurements across sampling locations, pyramid levels, boundary cases, precisions, and block sizes. The pseudocode also omits bilinear weights and boundary behavior, making this central claim difficult to audit.

The 8K accuracy conclusions rely on a newly generated, narrow test set: 332 adjacent pairs from only three sequences of one Blender movie, with forward flow only. Ground-truth construction is insufficiently validated, particularly its 16K-to-8K reduction, handling of occlusions/disocclusions and invalid pixels, and possible Blender motion-vector artifacts. Thus the claimed high-resolution state of the art has limited external validity.

Accuracy comparisons are not fully controlled. Methods use differing checkpoints or training regimes, FlowFormer uses its own tiling procedure, and the headline table compares the highest feasible resolution rather than a common scale or each method's accuracy-optimal operating point. For instance, several methods achieve lower EPE at reduced scale than at their highest feasible scale, complicating the SOTA framing.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript provides no concrete code or dataset release information, and key CUDA details—including cache remapping, allocation accounting, synchronization and timing protocol, and sparse kernel configuration—are underspecified. The statement that a block is formed from two B^4-by-D matrices also appears dimensionally incorrect; it should involve B^2 spatial features on each side and a B^2-by-B^2 output block.

The proposed sampler is not uniformly preferable: at ordinary resolutions it can be slower than dense sampling and uses substantially more memory than on-demand sampling, with large high-resolution memory variance. These trade-offs are visible in the tables, but the broad efficiency language should be restricted to memory-constrained, sufficiently high-resolution regimes.

strengths: The core systems contribution is useful and reasonably original: it exploits the spatial regularity and cross-iteration overlap of RAFT-style lookups using patch-major block sparsity and caching, while retaining the intended all-pairs lookup operation.

The efficiency evidence is broad. Isolated tests cover 1,041 Sintel pairs, resolutions through 8K, different feature dimensions and iteration counts, and four GPU classes. At 4096-pixel width, the sampler is 71–92% faster than on-demand computation across the reported GPUs while using far less memory than the dense implementation.

The paper demonstrates end-to-end relevance across RAFT, CCMR, MS-RAFT+, and SEA-RAFT. It makes otherwise-infeasible high-resolution configurations runnable and provides substantial speedups over on-demand sampling. The component breakdown also transparently exposes indexing and cache-management overhead.

The 8K evaluation addresses an underexplored practical regime. The training-free cascaded SEA-RAFT extension is simple and effective: at full resolution, it improves SEA-RAFT from 17.5% to 13.3% 1-pixel error and from 107.39 to 21.56 large-motion EPE.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes an algorithm overview, pseudocode, runtime decomposition, full per-scale results, and software and hardware settings. The principal runtime-memory tradeoff is supported convincingly.
weaknesses: Material: the claim of exactly matching the RAFT operator is not demonstrated rigorously enough. The paper mentions unit tests and reports a nonzero 0.03% endpoint-error difference, but provides no direct maximum or mean numerical error for the sampled correlations, boundary-case analysis, or downstream accuracy comparison among the dense, on-demand, and proposed implementations.

Material: the O(P^1.5) memory claim depends on choosing B=P^(1/8), whereas the experiments fix B to 8 or 16; with fixed B, the explicitly stored mask remains O(P^2). Equation (3) also incorrectly drops the square on the factor containing floor((K−1)/B). The asymptotic conclusion may still hold for fixed lookup radius under the proposed scaling, but it is overstated as a property of the evaluated implementation.

Material: the new benchmark comprises only 332 pairs from three shots of one synthetic movie and includes only forward flow. The manuscript does not validate the rendered motion vectors quantitatively, especially around occlusions and object boundaries. The large pixel count therefore does not provide broad scene diversity.

Material: the state-of-the-art accuracy claim is too broad. Cascaded SEA-RAFT wins the 1-pixel and large-motion metrics on the authors' dataset, but not overall EPE; for example, MS-RAFT+ reaches 1.63 EPE versus the cascaded method's best value of 1.90. Table 2 also compares methods at different feasible scales and with different training configurations.

The practical tradeoff is less uniform than the headline suggests. The cache can consume substantially more memory than on-demand sampling—for example, 66.68 versus 36.30 GiB for 8K CCMR—and the proposed implementation slows several models on Spring, Sintel, and KITTI by 4–23%. This does not negate its high-resolution value, but claims of similar memory and broad benefit need qualification.

Reproducibility needs improvement. Warm-up, GPU synchronization, clock control, and timing repetition details are underspecified; only one timed run is performed per image; flow resizing and vector scaling in cascaded inference are not fully formalized; and there is no explicit code or dataset release statement for the custom CUDA kernels and rendered benchmark. Notation and pseudocode inconsistencies are secondary presentation issues.

strengths: The block-sparse, incrementally cached sampler addresses a concrete RAFT bottleneck without changing the learned model or intended correlation lookup. The efficiency evidence is detailed and convincing. It covers resolution, iteration count, feature dimensionality, and four GPU classes. At width 4096 on GH200, the sampler takes 124 ms versus 1186 ms for on-demand computation while using about 2.9 GB rather than the dense implementation's roughly 71 GB.

End-to-end experiments establish practical value across RAFT, CCMR, MS-RAFT+, and SEA-RAFT. At full 8K, the method reduces RAFT runtime from 11.00 s to 4.59 s and SEA-RAFT runtime from 2.61 s to 1.90 s while remaining memory-feasible.

The 8K evaluation is valuable: it contains 332 forward-flow pairs and 9.3 billion evaluated pixels, compares many optical-flow systems over multiple scales, and separately measures large motion. The training-free cascaded SEA-RAFT procedure achieves strong accuracy, including 13.3% one-pixel error at full resolution and 18.61-pixel large-motion EPE at half resolution.

The paper is clear and technically informative, providing pseudocode, component timings, block-layout analysis, a memory derivation, qualitative comparisons, and explicit software and hardware settings.
weaknesses: The main material limitation is the narrow domain of the new benchmark: all 332 pairs come from three shots of one Blender movie. This supports the reported results on those scenes, but the broad state-of-the-art claim is less secure for diverse real UHR footage, camera motions, and rendering styles.

Exact operator equivalence is not demonstrated as directly as the central claim warrants. The paper reports unit tests and a 0.03% downstream EPE difference, but not elementwise agreement, maximum numerical error, precision settings, or boundary-case results.

The O(P^1.5) memory result depends on choosing block size B=P^(1/8) and treating the iteration count and lookup radius as constants, whereas experiments use fixed B=8 or 16. With fixed B, the mask remains asymptotically quadratic in P. The theoretical parameter schedule should be distinguished more clearly from the implemented scaling regime.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although the manuscript supplies pseudocode and experimental settings, it gives no explicit code or data release commitment and does not fully document motion-vector generation and validation. Reimplementing the custom CUDA kernels and benchmark would require substantial effort.

The cascaded comparison partly conflates the proposed inference policy with the underlying model: only SEA-RAFT receives recursive initialization, while competitors use standard inference. Ablations of recursion depth and the 800-pixel threshold, plus broader tests of comparable initialization, would better establish generality.

As a presentation refinement, the headline percentages use different baselines, and the main accuracy table mixes each competitor's highest feasible scale with two scales for the proposed cascade. Additional scale-matched summaries would make the comparison easier to interpret.
